stem: Which principle governed land acquisition in Zimbabwe's first ten years of independence?

options.content: Willing-seller, willing-buyer
options.rationale: Correct: required by the Lancaster House constitution.

options.content: Compulsory acquisition without any compensation
options.rationale: That was not allowed in the 1980s.

options.content: Land Apportionment by race
options.rationale: Racial land laws ended at independence.

options.content: Fifty-one per cent indigenous ownership
options.rationale: That is the indigenisation rule of 2007.

explanation: For ten years land could be bought only from owners who chose to sell, with adequate compensation.

stem: In which year was the Fast Track Land Reform Programme launched?

options.rationale: 1980 saw the start of willing-seller, willing-buyer resettlement.

explanation: The fast-track programme began in **2000**, after the February referendum and farm occupations.

stem: Why was land redistribution slow in the 1980s?

options.content: Very few African families wanted to farm in the 1980s
options.rationale: There was great demand for land.

options.content: Land could only be bought from willing sellers
options.rationale: Correct: offered land was often poor and costly.

options.content: The government had banned all resettlement
All white farmers had already left

explanation: Willing-seller, willing-buyer meant the government could buy only land that was offered, often expensive or poor, with limited funds.

stem: What was the difference between the A1 and A2 resettlement models?

options.content: A1 was for foreign companies; A2 was for families
A1 plots were in towns; A2 farms were in the rural areas
options.rationale: Both were agricultural resettlement in rural areas.

options.content: A1 was before 1980; A2 after 1980
options.rationale: Both were part of fast-track reform from 2000.

options.content: A1 gave smallholder plots; A2 gave commercial farms

explanation: A1 plots were for families with shared grazing; A2 farms were for those expected to farm commercially.

stem: What did the Indigenisation and Economic Empowerment Act of 2007 require?

options.content: Equal land shares for every citizen
51% indigenous ownership of larger firms
The return of all communal and resettlement land to chiefs
options.rationale: It did not deal with land allocation.

options.content: The closure of all foreign banks

explanation: Businesses above a set size had to be at least 51% owned by indigenous Zimbabweans; Community Share Ownership Trusts followed.

stem: How did the 2013 Constitution deal with compensation for land acquired for resettlement?

options.content: Full market value for land and improvements
options.rationale: Compensation is for improvements, not the land itself.

options.content: No compensation of any kind
Land returned to former owners
options.rationale: Land reform was entrenched, not reversed.

options.content: Paid for improvements, not the land

explanation: The Constitution vests acquired land in the state and provides compensation for improvements rather than for the land itself.
hints: Distinguish between the land and what was built on it.

stem: Which was a recognised problem of fast-track land reform?

options.content: No families received any land
options.rationale: Large numbers of families received land.

options.content: Tobacco growing was banned throughout Zimbabwe
options.rationale: Tobacco continued; smallholder output later grew.

options.content: Many farm workers lost jobs and homes
All land was given to foreign firms

explanation: Many farm workers lost employment and housing; other problems included falling output, lack of title and credit, and disputes.
hints: Think about people who lived and worked on commercial farms.

stem: Which statement best describes the debate about the measures Western countries took after 2000?

options.content: All sides agree the measures had no effect
The measures were imposed by the African Union and SADC jointly
options.rationale: They were imposed by the EU and USA.

options.content: The West calls them targeted; Zimbabwe calls them illegal
The measures were lifted in 2001

explanation: Western governments described their measures as targeted at individuals and concerns about governance; the Zimbabwean government called them illegal sanctions that harmed the whole economy.
hints: The question asks about the debate, not who is right.

stem: In February 2000 Zimbabwean voters rejected a draft constitution in a referendum.
explanation: True. Farm occupations followed, and the fast-track programme was launched in July 2000.

stem: Land reform in Zimbabwe began only in the year 2000.
explanation: False. Resettlement began in 1980 under willing-seller, willing-buyer; compulsory acquisition was allowed from 1992; fast track began in 2000.

stem: Match each law or document with what it did.

right.content: Required 51% indigenous ownership of larger businesses
Vested acquired land in the state; created a Land Commission
Protected property; willing-seller, willing-buyer for ten years

explanation: Each step changed the legal basis of land and economic ownership.

stem: Put these events in chronological order.

left.content: The Fast Track Land Reform Programme is launched
The Land Acquisition Act is passed
The Indigenisation and Economic Empowerment Act is passed
The donors' conference on land meets in Harare

explanation: Land Acquisition Act 1992; donors' conference 1998; fast track 2000; indigenisation act 2007.
hints: The Land Acquisition Act came two years after the Lancaster House restriction ended.

payload.template: The European Union imposed measures on Zimbabwe from {{blank:a}}. Zimbabwe left the {{blank:b}} in 2003.

explanation: EU measures began in 2002; Zimbabwe was suspended from the Commonwealth in 2002 and left in 2003.

stem: What percentage of ownership by indigenous Zimbabweans did the 2007 indigenisation law require of larger businesses? (Give a number.)
explanation: At least **51%**; the rule was narrowed in 2018.

stem: State **five** reasons for land reform in Zimbabwe.

points.description: Colonial land alienation and racial land laws (1930, 1969).
Unequal distribution at independence: best land held by a few thousand commercial farmers.
Land was a central aim of the liberation struggle.
Overcrowding and poor land in the communal areas.
Slow progress under willing-seller, willing-buyer / political pressure from war veterans and the landless.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Land had been taken under colonial rule and divided by race; in 1980 a few thousand farmers held much of the best land; land was a central aim of the liberation struggle; communal areas were crowded and poor; and willing-seller, willing-buyer resettlement was slow, increasing pressure from the landless and war veterans.

stem: Explain the benefits and problems of the Fast Track Land Reform Programme.

points.description: Benefit: large numbers of land-short families received land.
Benefit: wider ownership of farmland; many new farmers producing and investing.
Benefit: growth of smallholder tobacco production in the 2010s.
Problem: fall in commercial output and exports in the early 2000s; food shortages.
Problem: displacement of farm workers; violence on some farms.
Problem: lack of title, credit and inputs; multiple farm ownership; legal disputes.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Fast track gave land to large numbers of families who had been short of land, and farmland ownership spread from a small minority to many Zimbabweans; studies found many new farmers producing and investing, and smallholder tobacco grew strongly in the 2010s. However, commercial output and exports fell sharply in the early 2000s, contributing to food shortages. Many farm workers lost jobs and homes, and there was violence on some farms. New farmers often lacked title, credit and inputs, some prominent people received more than one farm, and legal disputes followed.

explanation: One mark per developed benefit or problem.
hints: Give three benefits and three problems, each explained.

stem: Explain **two** ways in which the Constitution affected land reform.

points.description: Identifies the Lancaster House restriction.
Explains: willing-seller, willing-buyer for ten years slowed redistribution in the 1980s.
Identifies later amendments / the 2013 Constitution.
Explains: allowed compulsory acquisition, compensation for improvements only, made reform hard to reverse.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The Lancaster House constitution required willing-seller, willing-buyer purchase for ten years, which slowed redistribution in the 1980s. Later amendments allowed compulsory acquisition and limited compensation to improvements, and the 2013 Constitution vested acquired land in the state, making land reform legally secure and hard to reverse.

hints: Think about the Constitution as both an obstacle and a tool.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — an interview with a fictional A1 farmer in Masvingo province, recorded by a researcher in 2012 (invented for this question)

> Before, we were eight families on two hectares in the communal lands, and the soil was finished. Now I have six hectares of my own. The first years were hard: no tractor, no seed, the rains failed twice. This season I sold tobacco and built a brick house. My children will not be squatters on their own land.

**Source B** — a report by a fictional business association in Harare, 2003 (invented for this question)

> Commercial agricultural output has collapsed. Banks will not lend to farmers without title deeds, exports have fallen, and thousands of farm workers have lost their jobs and homes. Investor confidence will not return while property rights are uncertain.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: According to Source A, how did land reform change the farmer's life?

points.description: More land (six hectares instead of a share of two).
Eventually higher income (sold tobacco, built a brick house).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far do Sources A and B agree about the effects of land reform?

points.description: Agree: early years were difficult (A's lack of tractor and seed; B's collapse of output).
Agree: problems of finance/inputs (A: no seed; B: no lending without title).
Disagree: A shows benefits to the new farmer; B shows only losses.
B mentions farm workers and investors, A does not; conclusion.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which source is more useful for assessing the outcomes of land reform? Use both sources and your own knowledge.

points.description: A: beneficiary's experience; one farmer, may be typical of some A1 areas (studies of Masvingo).
A: recorded in 2012, so shows longer-term recovery.
B: business association with an interest in property rights and investment.
B: 2003, during the worst period; accurate on falling output, workers displaced, lack of title.
Own knowledge: both benefits and problems recognised; debate continues.
Supported judgement: each useful for different aspects/times.

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source A is the account of a new A1 farmer recorded in 2012, so it shows the experience of a beneficiary over about ten years: more land, early hardship, and later success with tobacco. This matches studies that found many new farmers producing and investing, but it is one person's story. Source B comes from a business association in 2003, during the worst years, and reflects the interests of business and investors. Its points about falling output, displaced farm workers and the lack of title deeds for borrowing are supported by own knowledge. Each source is useful for a different aspect and moment: B for the early economic shock and its victims, A for the gains to new farmers in the longer term. Together they show why historians still debate the outcomes.

hints: Note the dates: the two sources look at different moments.

parts.stem: Describe the measures taken for indigenisation and gender equity in Zimbabwe.

points.description: Indigenisation and Economic Empowerment Act 2007: 51% indigenous ownership of larger firms.
Community Share Ownership Trusts / empowerment funds.
2013 Constitution: gender equality, 60 reserved National Assembly seats for women.
Zimbabwe Gender Commission / equal access to land.

parts.stem: How far did land reform achieve its aims?

points.description: Aim achieved: land redistributed to many families; colonial pattern of ownership changed.
Aim achieved: reform entrenched in the Constitution; later recovery in smallholder output.
Not achieved: fall in production and food security in the early 2000s.
Not achieved: farm workers displaced; lack of title/credit; multiple ownership; Western reaction and loss of investment.
Supported judgement.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Land reform aimed to correct the colonial division of land and give land to the landless. In this it largely succeeded: large numbers of families received land, the ownership of farmland changed from a small minority to a much wider group, and the 2013 Constitution made the reform hard to reverse. In some areas new farmers became productive, and smallholder tobacco production grew in the 2010s.

But land reform also aimed to improve livelihoods and the economy, and here the results were mixed. Commercial output and exports fell sharply in the early 2000s, contributing to food shortages. Many farm workers lost their jobs and homes, new farmers often lacked title, credit and inputs, and some prominent people gained more than one farm. Western criticism and measures reduced aid and investment.

Overall land reform achieved its central political aim of redistribution, but only partly achieved its economic aims; historians still debate how much of the decline was caused by the reform itself.

parts.explanation: Top level judges against the aims with both sides.

hints: In (b), consider the aims of land reform and judge against them.
